facts.text: Experts disagree on machine-learning classification under the Machinery Regulation: a capability-based reading counts any trained model, whereas a behaviour-based reading counts only models that change in service.
facts.quote: a capability-based reading (any trained model counts) versus a behaviour-based reading (only models that change in service count).

facts.text: The legitimacy of the MOSH collision-prevention blueprint as an industry specification is contested: a South African consultant's opinion piece questions whether the blueprint is valid without a regulator mandate, rather than treating the industry specification alone as valid.
facts.quote: a South African consultant's opinion piece questions whether the MOSH collision-prevention blueprint is valid unless mandated by the regulator.

facts.text: No source-attributable consensus exists on the acceptable trade-off between missed collisions and nuisance interventions: earlier intervention reduces collision risk but increases false braking, and an abrupt stop is itself hazardous on some machines.
facts.quote: no source-attributable consensus exists on the acceptable trade-off; earlier intervention cuts collision risk but raises false braking, and on some machines an abrupt stop is itself hazardous.

facts.text: The disputed balance between missed collisions and nuisance interventions depends on machine type, speed, payload, grade, articulation, nearby traffic and intervention level.
facts.quote: The balance depends on machine type, speed, payload, grade, articulation, nearby traffic and intervention level.

facts.text: AEB test stringency has sharply contrasting cost estimates: NHTSA's Final Regulatory Impact Analysis for FMVSS 127 estimates annual compliance costs of US$354.06 million in 2020 dollars, while a VBOX Automotive white paper contrasts that figure with an industry estimate of US$63 billion.
facts.quote: estimates compliance costs at 354.06 million US dollars a year (2020 dollars: 282.20 million for software on all vehicles plus 71.86 million for hardware on 5% of vehicles)

entities.name: NHTSA Final Regulatory Impact Analysis for FMVSS 127

facts.text: Within the disputed FMVSS 127 compliance-cost estimates, NHTSA's annual estimate in 2020 dollars assigns US$282.20 million to software on all vehicles and US$71.86 million to hardware on 5% of vehicles.
facts.quote: 2020 dollars: 282.20 million for software on all vehicles plus 71.86 million for hardware on 5% of vehicles

facts.text: A VBOX Automotive white paper calls both NHTSA's US$354.06 million annual FMVSS 127 compliance-cost estimate and the contrasting US$63 billion industry estimate "internally consistent"; that characterization was seen only in a search snippet.
facts.quote: a VBOX Automotive white paper contrasts this with an industry estimate of 63 billion US dollars, calling both "internally consistent" (seen in a search snippet only).

facts.text: Petitioners including the Alliance for Automotive Innovation and Volkswagen argued that FMVSS 127 compliance should be judged over multiple trials, whereas NHTSA rejected that position in its 26 November 2024 rule, Docket NHTSA-2023-0021, stating that FMVSS 127 testing "is distinct from FMVSS No. 135 testing".
facts.quote: NHTSA rejected this in its 26 November 2024 rule (Docket NHTSA-2023-0021), saying FMVSS 127 testing "is distinct from FMVSS No. 135 testing".

facts.text: The disagreement between per-trial AEB acceptance and statistical acceptance over multiple trials is likely to arise off-road as well as on-road.
facts.quote: The same per-trial versus statistical debate is likely off-road.

facts.text: South Africa's 2019 MRAC task team concluded that collision-prevention technology was not mature, yet the collision-prevention clauses were brought into force in December 2022.
facts.quote: South Africa's 2019 MRAC task team concluded collision-prevention technology was not mature, yet the clauses were brought into force in December 2022

facts.text: Against the bringing into force of South African collision-prevention clauses in December 2022 despite readiness concerns, EMESRT and ICMM material warns that unqualified Level 9 deployment can hurt production and accelerate brake wear.
facts.quote: EMESRT and ICMM material warns that unqualified Level 9 deployment can hurt production and accelerate brake wear.

facts.text: Against the claim that one sensor modality is inherently sufficient, no reviewed off-road rule supports that claim; camera, radar, lidar and ultrasonic sensors fail differently.
facts.quote: no reviewed off-road rule supports the claim that one modality is inherently sufficient; camera, radar, lidar and ultrasonic fail differently

facts.text: In the disagreement over inherent sufficiency of a sensor modality, MSHA's technology-neutral wording is consistent with arguing against the hazard rather than by technology label.
facts.quote: MSHA's technology-neutral wording is consistent with arguing against the hazard rather than by technology label.
